PullRequest.Title: launch: improve cross-platform setup and cleanup
PullRequest.Body: ## Summary - replace the Bash-only, `jq`-dependent Monaco paste implementation with a cross-platform Node helper - when authentication blocks launch automation, offer the user a choice between completing the current sign-in and bootstrapping the persistent source profile - keep persistent profile setup out of the normal launcher with small, dedicated Windows and macOS/Linux bootstrap scripts - add reliable Windows cleanup scoped to an isolated launch's exact user-data directory - document dependency-free JSON parsing and correct PowerShell forwarding of arguments after `--`

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The subprocess frequency, full-table scan, detached lifetime, and human-controlled duration are directly established by the changed script and bootstrap documentation. Exact per-scan CPU cost varies by OS and process count, which limits severity but not mechanism confidence.
Findings.PerformanceResource: A new `ps` subprocess plus full process-table parsing, arrays, and sets on every 250 ms timer tick
Findings.PerformanceScaling: The monitor launches four `ps` processes per second for the entire bootstrap-window lifetime (240 per minute); each invocation and the descendant-closure scan grow with the machine's process count and process-tree depth.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Persistent subprocess churn, CPU usage, scheduler wakeups, and battery drain while the user signs in or whenever the bootstrap Code OSS window is left open.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: The pre-diff documented bootstrap path launched Code OSS directly against the source profile and did not create a lifetime process-table monitor or recurring subprocesses.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Every successful macOS/Linux profile bootstrap now starts a detached Node monitor that synchronously spawns `ps`, parses the complete process table, and recomputes descendant/running sets four times per second after bootstrap readiness.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added line 71 places synchronous `execFileSync("ps", ...)` inside `check`, and added line 109 schedules `check` every 250 ms until every tracked Code OSS descendant exits.
Findings.Title: Defer process-table polling until the user waits for exit
Findings.Impact: Choosing profile bootstrap and taking several minutes to complete GitHub/Copilot sign-in produces hundreds to thousands of extra `ps` launches; leaving the persistent window open makes that overhead unbounded in time.
Findings.Evidence: `bootstrap-profile.sh` starts this detached monitor before waiting for CDP and returns JSON as soon as CDP is ready, while SKILL.md instructs the caller to wait for a human to sign in and close the window before invoking `--wait-for-exit`. Thus the 250 ms loop is active throughout a realistically long human interaction, not just a short shutdown check. The loop's expensive boundary and process-table cardinality are explicit in lines 66-75 and its lifetime condition is explicit in lines 100-111.
Findings.Recommendation: Avoid polling for the whole interactive session. Preserve the release guarantee with an OS lifecycle primitive/process-group owner, or perform a bounded, much lower-frequency targeted/profile-lock check only when `--wait-for-exit` is invoked after user acknowledgement.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The changed query, 250 ms cadence, detached ownership, and human-controlled lifetime are explicit. CIM query duration differs across Windows systems, so magnitude is uncertain, but repeated machine-wide IPC and allocation are certain.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Repeated CIM/WMI IPC queries that materialize every `Win32_Process`, followed by full-table arrays, hash sets, and descendant scans
Findings.PerformanceScaling: The added monitor issues four machine-wide CIM queries per second for as long as the bootstrap Code OSS process tree remains alive; work grows with both process count and the human-controlled window lifetime.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Ongoing CIM provider load, PowerShell CPU/allocation pressure, scheduler wakeups, and battery drain during profile sign-in or while the bootstrap window is left open.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this PR, users were instructed to launch `code.bat` directly against the persistent profile; that path had no hidden lifetime monitor and no recurring CIM process enumeration.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Every successful Windows profile bootstrap now launches a hidden PowerShell monitor that retrieves and materializes the complete system process table over CIM, rebuilds process sets, and rescans descendants four times per second until the entire Code OSS tree exits.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added line 19 executes `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` at the top of an unconditional loop, and added line 55 sleeps only 250 ms before repeating while any tracked process remains.
Findings.Title: Stop querying CIM four times per second for the window lifetime
Findings.Impact: A several-minute GitHub/Copilot sign-in causes hundreds or thousands of full `Win32_Process` queries, and an accidentally open bootstrap window sustains the machine-wide polling indefinitely.
Findings.Evidence: `bootstrap-profile.ps1` starts `windows-process-tree-monitor.ps1` as a detached hidden process and returns once `waitForCdp.ts` reports readiness. SKILL.md then waits on a user sign-in/close acknowledgement before checking the exit marker, proving that the unconditional CIM loop runs across the interactive interval rather than only during cleanup.
Findings.Recommendation: Replace steady-state CIM polling with a Windows lifecycle mechanism such as a job/process-exit notification, or defer a bounded, lower-frequency targeted/profile-use check to `-WaitForExit`; retain the exact-profile/process-tree release guarantee.

Scenarios.Scenario: Normal isolated launch from an existing authenticated profile on macOS/Linux or Windows
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Path validation, profile/shared-data copying, settings rewrite, pre-launch, Code OSS process start, and CDP readiness remain serial launch prerequisites. The added Unix `node -e` path normalization is one extra process on the critical path but is negligible relative to the unchanged launcher pipeline.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Stat/resolve the source profile and recursively copy its selected files and shared data
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One source check and one profile copy per launch, scaling with retained profile files; unchanged for an existing source profile
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The launcher already validated and copied the source profile before starting Code OSS.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Must finish before settings update and app startup

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Start Node to resolve the source path
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Exactly one Node process per Unix launch
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The shell previously tested the path directly without this Node invocation.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Adds one Node startup before profile preparation

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Run settings updater, optional pre-launch build preparation, Code OSS, and readiness helper
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One settings process, one optional pre-launch process, one app launch, and one readiness helper per launch; unchanged
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same subprocess chain ran for every successful launch.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: These dominate launch readiness but their frequency and placement are unchanged

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number and total bytes of files in the source profile/shared storage; the diff does not increase effective copy cardinality when the profile exists.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Profile preparation and pre-launch are serialized; the app and readiness probe overlap only after process start, unchanged from before.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Slim/full profile copies remain per-run with no shared cache. Pre-launch can still be skipped explicitly or benefit from existing build outputs; no cache key, hit, miss, or coalescing behavior changes.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence that successful existing-profile launches retain the prior expensive boundaries and gain only one fixed-cost Unix helper process.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The one added Node startup varies by platform but is dwarfed by profile copy and application startup.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: the only added work is one bounded path-normalization process, while the scaling profile-copy and startup paths are unchanged.

Scenarios.Scenario: Launch when the persistent source profile does not exist
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The launcher now creates an empty isolated profile, writes settings, runs pre-launch, starts Code OSS, and probes CDP; all must complete before the user can reach sign-in. Previously this scenario stopped at validation and could not make product progress.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Create the isolated profile/settings directories and write settings instead of copying a missing source
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: A fixed set of directories/files per launch; no source-tree copy
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The launcher exited before creating a runnable isolated profile.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Run pre-launch, start Code OSS, and poll its local CDP endpoint
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One pre-launch unless skipped, one app tree, one readiness helper, and serial localhost probes until ready or 90 seconds
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No app was launched because the missing profile caused immediate failure.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Defines time to the sign-in UI

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Build preparation state controls pre-launch duration; no source-profile collection is copied in this branch.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Directory/settings setup and pre-launch are serial; after app start, one readiness helper issues non-overlapping localhost probes.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Warm compiled outputs reduce pre-launch work and `--skip-prelaunch` remains available. The empty profile is intentionally fresh per run, with no negative-cache loop.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence that the diff intentionally replaces immediate failure with one complete launch.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Startup duration depends on build state, but the work is required to enable a previously blocked sign-in workflow.
Scenarios.Verdict: No performance finding: the added launch cost is the requested functionality and there was no previously progressing scenario whose latency regressed.

Scenarios.Scenario: Bootstrap a persistent profile, sign in interactively, close Code OSS, then wait for profile release
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Profile directory creation, Code OSS startup, and serial localhost CDP probes are required before the bootstrap command returns. The new process-tree monitors run concurrently and are off the readiness critical path, but continue consuming resources throughout the human sign-in interval. The final wait polls only an exit-marker file for up to 30 seconds.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Launch Code OSS against the persistent profile
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One application process tree per explicit bootstrap
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Documentation had the user launch Code OSS directly, so the same application boundary existed manually.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required to present sign-in UI; readiness waits for its CDP endpoint

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One non-overlapping HTTP request approximately every 100-300 ms until readiness, bounded by 90 seconds
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The manual setup instruction did not provide readiness synchronization.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Bootstrap output waits for the first successful response

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Spawn `ps` and parse the full process table every 250 ms
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Four subprocesses per second for the entire app lifetime; each scan scales with all machine processes
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Direct manual launch had no detached monitor or recurring `ps` subprocesses.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off the readiness critical path but concurrent with the app and user sign-in

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Query and materialize all `Win32_Process` instances over CIM every 250 ms
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Four machine-wide CIM queries per second for the entire app lifetime
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Direct `code.bat` launch had no hidden PowerShell/CIM monitor.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off the readiness critical path but competes for CPU/IPC resources during sign-in

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Test the exit marker during final wait
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Up to 120 file existence checks at 250 ms intervals, normally one after a completed close
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: There was no scripted release acknowledgement.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Blocks only the explicit post-close release check

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Machine process count and human-controlled bootstrap-window lifetime; monitor cost is O(processes × lifetime), with additional descendant-depth rescans.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One monitor per bootstrap. Each Unix `ps` or Windows CIM query is synchronous so ticks do not overlap, but monitoring overlaps the Code OSS workload and continues until every tracked descendant exits.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No process snapshot is cached or incrementally updated; every 250 ms tick refetches and rebuilds the complete process set. Exit-marker checks are uncached but bounded.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: Very high: cadence, full-table boundary, detached lifetime, and interactive duration are all explicit in changed code and documentation.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Per-scan cost varies with OS and process count, and users may sign in quickly, but several minutes is realistic and an unclosed window makes duration unbounded.
Scenarios.Verdict: Two medium findings submitted: recurring Unix `ps` subprocess churn and recurring Windows CIM process-table polling.

Scenarios.Scenario: Clean up an isolated Windows launch
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Optionally close one Playwright session, enumerate exact-profile Code OSS processes, stop matches with bounded retries, verify no matches remain, then recursively delete the run directory.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Invoke the local Playwright CLI to close a named session
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Zero or one CLI process per cleanup
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Runs before process termination but failure does not prevent cleanup

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Enumerate `Win32_Process` and parse command lines to find exact user-data arguments
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Two scans when no process remains; at most six scans across five stop attempts plus verification
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Users manually killed the returned wrapper PID and removed the directory, which was unreliable on Windows.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Serial and required to avoid deleting a profile still in use

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Recursively delete the isolated run directory
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One successful recursive delete, with at most five serialized attempts

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of matching Code OSS processes and files in one isolated run directory; process scans are capped and exact-profile filtered.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: All cleanup actions and retries are serialized; no burst or unbounded queue is introduced.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache is relevant. Process state is intentionally refreshed between bounded termination attempts; package resolution uses the repository's installed Playwright dependency.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence that all new expensive boundaries are bounded and scoped to one cleanup operation.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: CIM and deletion latency vary with machine load/profile size, but retry counts are fixed and cleanup is an explicit teardown path.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: the work is bounded teardown necessary for reliable Windows cleanup, not a hot or lifetime path.

Scenarios.Scenario: Paste text into a chat Monaco editor through Playwright
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Focus the chat input, optionally send select-all and backspace, write/run one temporary paste script, parse its result, and remove the temporary directory. These operations are serialized before the caller can submit the prompt.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Run Playwright CLI commands through direct Node entrypoint
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Two calls when appending (focus and paste), four in default replace mode (focus, two keypresses, paste)
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The Bash implementation made the same two/four CLI calls through `npx`, plus separate Node and jq processes.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Every call is serial and required before paste completion

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Create a temporary directory, write one generated JavaScript file, and recursively remove it
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The old helper passed generated JavaScript inline and did not create this temporary file.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The file is required by `run-code`; cleanup happens before result parsing

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Execute focus, keypress, DOM paste, and verification through the existing Playwright/CDP session
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Same command count as before; verification is capped at 20 attempts and scans rendered view lines
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Equivalent focus, keypress, paste event, and capped rendered-line verification ran through the Bash helper.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Defines paste latency, unchanged in effective cardinality

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Prompt bytes and rendered view-line count; verification remains capped at 20 attempts and uses only a 40-character expected prefix.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: CLI operations are strictly serial with no new fan-out. One helper process handles argument parsing and result parsing.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The helper resolves the installed CLI module once per paste process and reuses that path for all calls. There is no cross-invocation cache, matching the old process-per-invocation behavior.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence that effective CLI cardinality and DOM work are preserved while package-launch overhead is reduced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Temporary-file latency varies by filesystem, but it replaces shell/inline-command and jq overhead and is fixed at one small file.
Scenarios.Verdict: No performance finding: the rewrite does not amplify subprocess, IPC, DOM, or verification cardinality, and the new temporary-file work is bounded.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 10 changed files and all diff pages. Submitted two high-confidence medium findings for unbounded-lifetime process-table polling in the new Unix and Windows bootstrap monitors; other changed launch, cleanup, and paste paths are bounded, intentional, or preserve prior expensive-boundary cardinality.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
